questions.question: Was Jesus really God, or just a good teacher?
questions.shortAnswer: The 'good teacher' option is the one the evidence does not allow, because Jesus claimed an identity no merely good teacher would claim. Christians believe he was telling the truth.
questions.answer:
There is a popular middle position that Jesus was a great moral teacher, a wise man, but not divine. It sounds humble and generous. C.S. Lewis pointed out that it is the one option Jesus himself does not leave open. A merely great teacher does not forgive sins committed against other people, accept worship, claim to existed before Abraham, and say that he and the Father are one. A man who said those things while being only a man would be either a liar, or a lunatic on the level of someone claiming to be a poached egg, or else he was telling the truth. The polite third category, good teacher, is not on the menu.

The claims are scattered all through the earliest material, not invented centuries later. He receives worship and does not stop it, which a faithful Jew would have found blasphemous. He applies to himself the divine name from Exodus, I am. He forgives sins, and his critics rightly note that only God can do that. The scholar Richard Bauckham has shown that the first Christians, who were monotheistic Jews, did the unthinkable almost immediately: they included Jesus inside the identity of the one God of Israel, worshiping him without believing they had abandoned their monotheism.

The formal language came later, but it was defending what was already there, not inventing something new. At the Council of Nicaea in 325 the church confessed the Son to be of one substance with the Father against the teaching of Arius, who held that there was a time when the Son was not. At Chalcedon in 451 it confessed Jesus to be fully God and fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion and without division. These councils were guardrails around a mystery the church had been living inside from the start.

Why does it matter whether he was only a teacher or actually God? Because if he was only a teacher, he left advice, and we have plenty of advice. If he was God in the flesh, then in him the maker of the universe has a human face, and his death is not a tragedy but a rescue, and his words are not suggestions but the voice of the one who made you. Everything hangs on it. The question is not whether Jesus was nice. It is whether he was who he said he was.

questions.question: How do we know Jesus actually rose from the dead?
questions.shortAnswer: No one can hand you a video, but the historical case rests on facts most scholars grant and asks which explanation accounts for all of them. The empty tomb and the changed witnesses are hard to dismiss.
questions.answer:
Christianity is unusual among religions in that it stakes everything on a historical claim that could, in principle, be falsified. Paul says it without hedging: if Christ has not been raised, our faith is worthless and we are to be pitied. So the resurrection is not a symbol the faith could survive without. It is the load-bearing wall.

Historians who study the period, believing and skeptical alike, tend to agree on a short list of facts that any theory has to explain. Jesus was executed by crucifixion and buried. His tomb was found empty. His followers, and at least two skeptics, James his brother and Paul his persecutor, had experiences they were certain were encounters with him alive. And the movement exploded in the very city where his body could have been produced to end it, and never was. Gary Habermas built much of his work around this minimal-facts approach, granting only what the broad scholarly consensus grants.

The alternative explanations are old and each one strains. The disciples lied: but people do not endure torture and death for what they know to be a hoax, and nearly all of them did. They hallucinated: but groups do not share the same detailed hallucination over weeks, and hallucinations do not leave an empty tomb. The authorities moved the body: then producing it would have strangled the church in its crib. Notice too that the first witnesses named are women, whose testimony carried little legal weight in that world. No one inventing a story for first-century readers would build it on witnesses no one was expected to believe. That detail smells like memory, not marketing.

The historian N.T. Wright, in a nearly eight-hundred-page study, argues that neither pagan nor Jewish expectation can account for what the first Christians claimed. Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the world, of everyone at once. Nobody expected one man to rise in the middle of history. Something happened that forced them to revise a belief they had held for centuries.

None of this compels faith, and it is not meant to. It is meant to clear the ground of the idea that only the gullible could believe it. The question the empty tomb leaves you with is not whether intelligent people can hold this. They can and do. The question is what you will do if it is true.

questions.question: How can God be three and one at the same time?
questions.shortAnswer: Christians do not claim God is three of the same thing and one of the same thing, which would be a contradiction. We claim one God in three persons, which is a mystery the church confesses without pretending to exhaust it.
questions.answer:
The Trinity is the doctrine everyone assumes is the most abstract and impractical, and it is actually the most important thing Christianity says about who God is. The claim is precise: there is one God, who exists eternally as three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, each fully God, yet not three Gods. It is not a riddle invented to confuse you. It is the church refusing to let go of things the Bible would not let it let go of.

Two guardrails define it. The first is against tritheism, the idea of three Gods, which the Bible's relentless monotheism forbids: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. The second is against modalism, the idea that God is one person wearing three masks at different times, which fails because the Father, Son, and Spirit speak to one another and love one another in the same scenes. At the baptism of Jesus, the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks from heaven. That is one moment, three persons.

The formal vocabulary was hammered out under pressure. At Nicaea in 325 the church rejected Arius and confessed the Son as of one substance with the Father. The Cappadocian fathers in the fourth century gave the language of one essence in three persons. Augustine, in his great work on the Trinity, warned that every analogy breaks: the water-ice-steam picture drifts toward modalism, the three-leaf clover toward tritheism. The Greek tradition spoke of perichoresis, the eternal mutual indwelling, the persons making room for one another in a kind of eternal dance.

Here is why it is not abstract at all. If God were a single solitary person, then before he made the world he was alone, and love would be something he learned by creating, something he needed us for. But if God is eternally three persons giving themselves to one another, then love is not something God does. It is what God is, before the universe existed, with no need of us at all. When the Bible says God is love, the Trinity is what makes that sentence true rather than sentimental. You were made by a community of self-giving love, and made for it.

questions.question: Why did Jesus have to die?
questions.shortAnswer: Because sin is a real debt against a real God, and Jesus chose to pay it himself rather than leave us to. The cross is where God's justice and God's mercy meet instead of cancel each other.
questions.answer:
Why did Jesus have to die is really two questions. Why did they kill him, and why did God will it. The first is history. The second is the heart of the gospel.

The historical answer is plain enough. Jesus threatened the religious establishment by claiming an authority that belonged to God alone, and he threatened Rome by being hailed as a king. A coalition of frightened power did what frightened power does. But the New Testament insists the cross was not merely a miscarriage of justice that God reacted to. It was, somehow, the plan, foreshadowed for centuries, the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world.

So why would God will it. The Bible piles up images rather than a single equation, and the wisest theologians have held several together. The oldest is substitution: we owed a debt we could not pay, and Jesus paid it in our place, the just for the unjust, taking the judgment our sin had earned so that we would not have to. Anselm, in the eleventh century, framed it in terms of a debt to God's honor; the Reformers in terms of the law's penalty borne by a willing substitute. Alongside that runs the image of victory, what the old church called Christus Victor, the cross as the battlefield where Christ defeated sin, death, and the powers, looking like defeat and being the decisive win. And there is the image of love's demonstration, God proving once and for all the lengths to which he would go, dying for his enemies while they were still his enemies.

These are not rival theories so much as facets of one jewel. Strip out substitution and the cross becomes a moving gesture that accomplishes nothing real. Strip out love and it becomes a cold transaction. Hold them together and you get the scandal at the center of the faith: the Judge stepped down from the bench and took the sentence himself.

This is why Christians cannot treat the cross as a sad preliminary to Easter. It is the place where the holiness of God and the love of God meet without either being compromised. Justice is satisfied and mercy is poured out in the same act. That is what had to happen, and it is what did.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians describe how the cross works in more than one way, from substitution to victory over evil to a demonstration of love, and most hold these together rather than choosing only one.

questions.question: Is Jesus really the only way to God?
questions.shortAnswer: Christians hold that Jesus is the one savior of the world, not because Christianity is one club among many, but because of who they believe Jesus is. If he is God come to rescue us, then he is not one road among several.
questions.answer:
This is the claim the modern world finds most offensive: Jesus saying I am the way, the truth, and the life, no one comes to the Father except through me. It sounds arrogant, even dangerous, in a society that prizes tolerance above almost everything. The objection deserves a real answer, not a softening.

Start by noticing that the popular alternative is not as humble as it looks. The famous picture is several blind men touching different parts of an elephant, each grasping only a piece, none seeing the whole. It is meant to teach humility. But to tell the story you have to be the one person in the room who can see the whole elephant and knows the blind men are mistaken. The pluralist who says all religions are partial glimpses of the same truth has quietly claimed the very thing he denies to everyone else, a view from above. Lesslie Newbigin, who spent decades as a missionary in India among genuinely devout people of other faiths, saw this clearly. There is no neutral ground. Everyone is standing somewhere.

It also helps to see that the religions are not in fact saying the same thing. They make contradictory claims about the most basic questions, whether God is personal, whether the self is real, what is wrong with us, and what the rescue is. They cannot all be true at once any more than contradictory maps can all lead home. Respecting them means taking their differences seriously, not flattening them into a vague sameness none of their adherents would recognize.

What makes the Christian claim bearable, even good, is its content. Christianity does not say we are the way because our group is superior or our morality is better. It says no one climbs to God, that all our climbing falls short, and that God came down. The exclusivity is not a velvet rope around a club. It is a rescue in a single lifeboat. Tim Keller noted that a truly narrow, self-righteous religion produces proud people, while the message of a God crucified for his enemies, if you actually believe it, produces the humblest people on earth, because it tells you that you are saved by sheer mercy and not by being right.

And the door is wider than the offense suggests. The one way is not a wall to keep people out. It is a person with his arms open, and the invitation in the last page of the Bible is simple: let the one who is thirsty come.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Faithful Christians agree Christ is the one savior but differ on the fate of those who never hear of him, a question taken up in the next entry.

questions.question: What about people who never heard of Jesus?
questions.shortAnswer: This is one of the most pressing questions a thoughtful person can ask, and Scripture does not give a tidy formula. What it does promise is that the Judge of all the earth will do right.
questions.answer:
What about the person who lived and died having never heard of Jesus, through no fault of their own. This is not a debating trick. It is one of the most pressing moral questions the faith faces, and the honest answer begins with humility about how much we are told.

Start with what is clear. The Bible says God is perfectly just and also genuinely good, that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and that he is the judge of all the earth who will do right. Whatever happens to the unevangelized, it will not be unfair. The Judge can be trusted even where the verdict is hidden from us. That alone answers the emotional force of the question, even before the theology.

Scripture also says that no one is a blank slate. Paul argues that creation itself testifies to a Creator, and that conscience writes a moral law on every heart, so that people are responsible for what they do with the light they have, however dim. No one is judged for rejecting a name they never heard. People are judged for what they did with what they were given.

From there, faithful Christians divide, and it is worth knowing the range. The restrictivist view holds that explicit faith in Christ is necessary, which makes the missionary task urgent. The inclusivist view, held by figures as orthodox as C.S. Lewis, holds that Christ is still the only Savior, but that God may apply that salvation to some who responded to the light they had without knowing his name, the way Old Testament believers were saved by a Christ they could not yet see. There is also a strong biblical theme that God moves heaven and earth to get the gospel to those who are seeking, sending a Philip to the one Ethiopian on the road.

What all faithful positions refuse is the cynicism that says it does not matter, and the arrogance that says we have God's filing system memorized. Salvation is through Christ alone. How widely God applies that, in cases we cannot see, we leave to a Judge who loved the world enough to die for it. And we let the weight of the question do what it is meant to do: send us to tell people, rather than to speculate about them.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Some hold explicit faith in Christ is necessary for salvation, others that God may justly save some who never heard through Christ's work on the basis of the light they were given, with various positions in between, while all agree salvation comes only through Christ.

questions.question: Aren't all religions basically saying the same thing?
questions.shortAnswer: They share real moral wisdom, and that common ground is worth honoring. But on the questions that matter most, who God is and how we are made right with him, they say genuinely different things.
questions.answer:
It is true that the great faiths often agree about kindness, honesty, generosity, and the dignity of human life. That overlap is not nothing. A person who treats those agreements as a sign of shared conscience is seeing something true. We should not flatten other believers into caricatures or pretend they teach nothing good.

But to say all religions are the same is, in its own way, disrespectful to each of them. It tells the Muslim, the Hindu, the Buddhist, and the Jew that the very thing they hold most precious does not really matter. They would not recognize themselves in the claim that the differences are cosmetic.

The differences are real and they are deep. Is God personal or impersonal. Is the human problem ignorance, or imbalance, or guilt before a holy God. Is salvation something we achieve or something we receive. These are not the same answer in different clothes. They are different answers, and they cannot all be true at once.

Respecting another faith means taking its actual claims seriously enough to disagree where you must. The Christian claim is specific. God came to us in Jesus and did for us what we could not do for ourselves. That is either true or it is not, and it is worth examining on its own terms rather than dissolving into a vague sameness no one actually believes.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians agree the faiths genuinely differ on God and salvation, while differing among themselves over how much truth God has made available within other religious traditions.

questions.question: What is grace, really?
questions.shortAnswer: Grace is God giving you what you have not earned and could never earn. Not a reward for the good. A gift for the undeserving, which is everyone.
questions.answer:
We use the word grace for graceful dancers and gracious hosts, and we lose what it meant. Grace is favor you did not earn and cannot pay back. It runs against every instinct we have, because we are built to keep score.

Religion, at its worst, is a ladder. Do more, sin less, climb higher, and maybe God will be pleased. Grace cuts the ladder down. It says the climbing was never going to work, and God came down to you instead. You are accepted first, and the obedience grows out of the acceptance, not the other way around.

This is why grace offends respectable people more than it offends sinners. The sinner knows he needs a gift. The respectable man wants a wage. But God does not pay wages for righteousness, because none of us has earned one.

You are loved at your worst. That is not permission to stay there. It is the only thing strong enough to change you.

questions.question: If I am forgiven, why do I still sin?
questions.shortAnswer: Because forgiveness and full healing are not the same moment. You are pardoned now, and you are being remade slowly. The war you feel is evidence you are alive, not proof you are fake.
questions.answer:
Many Christians carry a quiet panic. They were told that meeting Jesus would fix them, and then they kept failing, and they wondered if it ever took. It took. You are just feeling something the New Testament describes plainly.

The Bible draws a line between justification, being declared right with God in an instant, and sanctification, being made actually holy over a lifetime. The first is finished. The second is in progress. You are pardoned fully and healed gradually, and the gap between those two is where the struggle lives.

Paul, near the end of his life, still wrote about doing the thing he hated. That was not a young convert. That was an apostle. The presence of the fight is not the absence of grace. A dead man does not struggle against sin. The struggle itself is a sign the Spirit is in you.

So do not measure your standing by your feelings on a bad day. Measure it by the cross. Then get up and keep walking. Slow growth is still growth.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how much victory over sin to expect in this life. Some traditions emphasize ongoing struggle until death, others a deeper work of the Spirit that breaks sin's grip more decisively. All agree perfection waits for the resurrection.

questions.question: Is it okay to be angry at God?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes. The Bible is full of people who told God exactly how they felt. He can hold your anger. What he asks is that you bring it to him instead of walking away.
questions.answer:
Somewhere we picked up the idea that good faith is calm faith, that real believers do not get angry with God. The Bible never says this. A third of the Psalms are complaints, and some of them are furious.

Job accused God to his face. Jeremiah said God had deceived him. The Psalmist asked how long, over and over, with no answer in sight. None of them were struck down for it. The honesty was counted as faith, because they were still talking to God, not about him from a distance.

There is a difference between anger that turns toward God and anger that turns away. The first is prayer, even when it shakes. The second is the slow drift into a closed heart. God can take the shouting. What grieves him is the silence of a person who has decided he is not worth the conversation.

So say it. Tell him where it hurts and why you are angry. The door he wants open is the one you slam when you go quiet.

questions.question: What is heaven actually like?
questions.shortAnswer: Less like clouds and harps than you were told. The Christian hope is not floating spirits but a renewed creation, resurrected bodies, and God dwelling with his people on a healed earth.
questions.answer:
Ask most people to picture heaven and they imagine disembodied souls on clouds, which sounds boring because it would be. That picture owes more to cartoons than to Scripture.

The Bible's hope is louder and more physical than that. It ends not with us escaping to heaven but with heaven coming down, a new heaven and a new earth, the city of God on a renewed creation. The dead are not left as ghosts. They are raised, given bodies like the risen Jesus, who ate fish after he rose.

What makes it heaven is not the architecture. It is the presence. The promise is that God will dwell with his people, wipe every tear, and end death itself. Everything that breaks here will be mended there, and the mending will be permanent.

So the Christian does not hope to leave the world behind forever. He hopes for the world made right, with the curtain between God and us finally torn down for good.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on the details and timing of the end, and on how literally to read the imagery in Revelation. The core they share is bodily resurrection, a renewed creation, and unbroken life with God.

questions.question: Why did God command the killing of the Canaanites?
questions.shortAnswer: It is one of the hardest passages in the Bible, and it should not be smoothed over. There are honest things to say about judgment, the language of the ancient world, and Jesus, but no answer that makes it comfortable.
questions.answer:
This is the question that makes thoughtful readers close the Bible, and pretending it is easy does more harm than the question does. So start by admitting it is terrible to read.

A few things belong in the room. The conquest is framed as judgment on generations of entrenched evil, including child sacrifice, not as ethnic hatred. The language of total destruction was a known ancient way of describing decisive defeat, and the same books that say all were destroyed go on to describe survivors, which suggests the rhetoric was not a literal body count. And this was a specific, bounded command tied to one moment in redemptive history, never a standing pattern for God's people.

None of that dissolves the horror, and it should not. What it does is locate it. The deepest Christian answer is not a clever defense but a person. The God who is revealed fully in Jesus weeps at tombs, dies for his enemies, and tells his followers to put the sword away. Whatever we make of Joshua, we read it back through Calvary, not the other way around.

Hold the tension honestly. A faith that can only survive by hiding its hardest pages is not worth much. This one does not ask you to hide them.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ widely here: some read the conquest accounts as largely hyperbolic ancient war language, some emphasize divine judgment on specific evil, some wrestle with it as a genuine moral difficulty held in tension with the character of Christ. Faithful readers land in different places.

questions.question: Why are there so many Bible translations, and which one is right?
questions.shortAnswer: Because translating ancient languages forces real choices between word-for-word precision and natural readability. The differences are mostly about style, not message. Pick a trustworthy one you will actually read.
questions.answer:
Walk into a bookstore and the wall of Bibles can feel like a reason to doubt. If the experts cannot agree on the words, how can any of it be trusted? But the variety is a sign of care, not confusion.

Every translation sits somewhere on a line. On one end is word-for-word, which keeps the original structure but can read stiffly. On the other is thought-for-thought, which reads smoothly but makes more interpretive calls for you. A paraphrase goes further still, restating ideas in fresh language. None of these is dishonest. They are answering the same question differently: how do you carry meaning across a few thousand years and a very different language.

What matters is that the core is stable across all of them. No doctrine of the faith rises or falls on which mainstream translation you hold. The places that differ are mostly matters of phrasing, and good Bibles footnote the genuinely uncertain spots openly.

So do not let the wall paralyze you. Choose a respected translation in language you understand, and then do the one thing all the arguing can distract you from. Read it.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on translation philosophy and on which manuscript traditions to prefer. A minority hold to a single translation as uniquely faithful. Most hold that several reliable translations, read together, serve the church well.

questions.question: Is there any real evidence Jesus even existed?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes, and it is not close. The existence of Jesus of Nazareth is one of the best-attested facts of ancient history, accepted by nearly all historians, believing or not.
questions.answer:
Online you will meet the claim that Jesus is a myth, a character invented whole. It feels bold and skeptical. It is also a position almost no working historian holds, including the ones with no faith to defend.

The evidence is unusually strong for an ancient figure. We have multiple early Christian sources written within a generation of his life, by people in a position to know. We also have hostile and neutral non-Christian witnesses, the Roman historian Tacitus and the Jewish historian Josephus among them, who refer to Jesus, his execution under Pilate, and the movement that followed. People do not invent and then die for a person they know never lived.

Notice the real debate. Serious historians argue about who Jesus was and what his life meant, not whether he was there. The question Did he exist is settled. The question Who is he is the one that actually costs you something.

That is the better place to spend your doubt. Not on whether the man walked, but on what to do with the things he said.

questions.question: Why are there so many denominations?
questions.shortAnswer: Some of it is sin and pride, and we should own that. Some of it is honest disagreement over real questions. Underneath the divisions, the historic church shares one core faith.
questions.answer:
Thousands of denominations look like a scandal, and at times they are exactly that. Christians have split over ego, power, and culture as often as over conviction, and the watching world is right to wince. We should not defend every division.

But not all of it is failure. Some of the branches grew from genuine questions that thoughtful believers answered differently. How should we baptize. How is Christ present in communion. Who governs the church. These are not trivial, and good people, reading the same Bible prayerfully, have landed in different places.

It helps to sort beliefs by weight. There is a center the historic church has always shared, the Trinity, the deity and resurrection of Christ, salvation by grace, the authority of Scripture. Then there is a second ring of important matters where faithful Christians divide, and a third ring of preferences that should never divide anyone. Most denominational lines are drawn in the second ring.

So do not let the map of divisions hide the one faith underneath it. The body of Christ is larger and more united than the directory of churches makes it look.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The disagreements behind denominations are themselves what Christians differ on: baptism, the Lord's Supper, church government, the gifts of the Spirit, and more. The point is not that these do not matter, but that they sit a ring out from the shared core.

questions.question: What is baptism, and do I need to be baptized?
questions.shortAnswer: Baptism is the sign Jesus gave for entering his people, a public washing that pictures dying and rising with him. The New Testament treats it as the normal next step for a believer, not an optional extra.
questions.answer:
Baptism can feel like an old ritual we keep out of habit, but Jesus commanded it, and the early church never treated it as decoration. It was how you crossed the line from outsider to belonging.

The picture is rich. Going under the water is a kind of burial, coming up a kind of resurrection, your old life left behind and a new one begun in Christ. It is also a public confession. In the first century, to be baptized was to declare a loyalty that could cost you your family or your life. It was never meant to be private.

So if you have trusted Christ and never been baptized, the New Testament's expectation is plain. This is the normal next step, the front door of the visible church, not an advanced option for the especially serious.

It does not earn you anything. It announces something already true and binds you publicly to the people of God. Do not skip the doorway Jesus built.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on who should be baptized and how. Some baptize the infant children of believers, trusting the covenant promise, and some baptize only those who personally profess faith. Some immerse, some pour or sprinkle. They share the conviction that baptism is Christ's appointed sign of belonging.

questions.question: Why is the church so full of hypocrites?
questions.shortAnswer: Partly because the church is a hospital, not a museum, so of course it is full of sick people. And partly because some of the wounds are real, and pretending otherwise is its own hypocrisy.
questions.answer:
It is a fair complaint, and the worst response is a defensive one. Yes, the church is full of hypocrites. There is always room for one more, which is why the door is open.

A church is not a display case for finished people. It is closer to a hospital, a place where the sick gather precisely because they are sick. A waiting room full of coughing patients does not disprove medicine. A church full of struggling people does not disprove the gospel. It is what you would expect from a community whose entry requirement is admitting you need help.

But some of the anger is not about ordinary failure. It is about real harm done by people who claimed the name of Christ, the abuse covered up, the pride dressed as holiness, the cruelty defended with verses. That is not the gospel failing. That is the gospel betrayed, and Jesus said harder things about religious hypocrites than any skeptic ever has.

So bring the complaint to Jesus, not just about him. He shares it. And measure the faith by the one who founded it, not only by the ones who have failed it, yourself and me included.

questions.question: Is it a sin to doubt?
questions.shortAnswer: No. Doubt is not the opposite of faith, certainty is not the same as faith, and Scripture treats honest questions with patience. What you do with the doubt is what matters.
questions.answer:
Many people raised in the church learned that questions were dangerous, that a good Christian simply believes. So when the doubts came, they felt like betrayal, and the shame drove them into hiding, where doubt always grows worst.

But the Bible does not flinch at doubt. Thomas asked for proof and got it. John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask whether Jesus was really the one, and Jesus did not scold him, he reassured him. A father once cried out, I believe, help my unbelief, and Jesus healed his son anyway. Honest doubt brought into the open is treated with patience, not punishment.

There is a kind of doubt that is really a refusal, a heart that has decided and is only collecting excuses. That is different. But the doubt of someone who desperately wants it to be true and cannot yet see, that is not sin. That is faith under strain, and strain is not the same as falling.

So do not hide it. Doubt expressed to God in the company of honest people tends to grow toward faith. Doubt buried in shame and faced alone tends to rot. Bring it into the light.
questions.doctrineTitle: What Is the Bible, and Can We Trust It?

questions.question: I am deconstructing my faith. Is that wrong?
questions.shortAnswer: It depends on what you are taking apart and why. Examining what you were taught can be honest and even healthy. The danger is mistaking the tearing down for a destination.
questions.answer:
The word deconstruction now covers everything from leaving the faith to finally thinking it through, so the first honest move is to ask what you actually mean.

Some of what people pull apart deserves it. They were handed a tangle of real gospel and cultural baggage, political loyalty, family control, fear dressed as faith, and they are trying to separate the treasure from the wrapping. That work is not rebellion. It can be obedience, the slow labor of loving God with your mind instead of inheriting a faith you never examined.

The danger is in treating demolition as the goal. A house torn down is not a place to live. If the whole project is unending suspicion, where every belief is guilty until proven innocent and nothing is ever rebuilt, it does not end in freedom. It ends in a cold and empty lot. Tearing down is a phase, not a home.

So take it apart honestly, with people who will not panic and will not lie to you. But aim to rebuild on what is actually true, not merely to be free of what was false. The goal is a faith that can hold weight, not no faith at all.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians use deconstruction to mean very different things, and assess it differently as a result. Some see it mainly as a needed sifting of cultural distortions, others warn it often slides into abandoning the faith. Discernment depends on what is being questioned and where it lands.
questions.doctrineTitle: What Is the Bible, and Can We Trust It?

questions.question: How do I believe when I do not feel anything?
questions.shortAnswer: Faith is not a feeling, and the absence of feeling is not the absence of faith. Trust is something you do, often in the dark, and the feelings frequently follow rather than lead.
questions.answer:
There are seasons when prayer feels like talking to the ceiling and worship moves nothing in you. People in these seasons often assume their faith has died. Usually it has not. They have just confused faith with its weather.

Feelings are real and they matter, but they are responses, not the foundation. The Bible roots faith in what is true and what God has done, not in the temperature of your heart on a given morning. Some of the most faithful people in Scripture served God through long stretches of silence and dryness, and the obedience held even when the warmth did not.

There is even a mercy in the dry seasons. They burn off the part of faith that was only ever in it for the feeling, and they teach you to trust the One you cannot feel. A love that only works when it is exciting is not yet mature love. The same is true with God.

So keep showing up. Pray when it is flat, gather when you would rather not, obey when nothing stirs. Faith is loyalty in the dark, and the feelings tend to return to the person who kept walking without them.

questions.question: Is the gospel political?
questions.shortAnswer: It is political in that it announces a King and a kingdom that claim all of life. It is not partisan. The moment the gospel becomes a mascot for your party, you have traded it for something smaller.
questions.answer:
People mean two different things by political, and the confusion does real damage. If political means belonging to a party, the gospel is not that. If it means having public consequences, the gospel is unavoidably that.

The earliest Christian confession, Jesus is Lord, was a political sentence in a world where Caesar claimed that title. To say Jesus is King is to say no one else finally is, not the emperor, not the market, not the nation. That claim reshapes how you hold money, power, enemies, and the poor. It will not stay safely inside the church walls.

But the same gospel refuses to be captured by a tribe. The instant it becomes a chaplain blessing one party and damning the other, it stops being the gospel and becomes a campaign. The cross stands over every flag, and it judges the left and the right alike. Both are happy to use Jesus. Neither gets to own him.

So let it make you a difficult voter, loyal to a kingdom that no earthly party fully represents. Not above the fray out of cowardice. Engaged, but never owned.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians sharply disagree about how faith should shape political engagement, which issues weigh most, and how involved the church should be. The shared conviction is that Christ, not any party, holds final allegiance.

questions.question: What does the Bible actually mean by justice?
questions.shortAnswer: Far more than punishing crime. Biblical justice means rendering to each what they are due and lifting the burden off the vulnerable, woven all through the law and the prophets and the heart of God.
questions.answer:
Justice has become a word people fight over, claimed by one side and feared by the other, and in the noise its biblical meaning gets lost. Scripture is not shy about it. The word runs from Genesis to Revelation.

In the Bible, justice is bigger than a courtroom. The Hebrew words gather up two ideas, mishpat, treating people fairly and giving them their due, and tsedaqah, a right ordering of relationships and society. God ties them together and ties them to himself. He repeatedly identifies as the defender of the people most easily crushed, named again and again as the orphan, the widow, the foreigner, and the poor.

This is not a modern political program smuggled into the text. It is the text. The prophets thundered at worshipers who kept the festivals while grinding the faces of the poor, and God said he hated their religious services because of it. Care for the vulnerable was never optional decoration on the faith. It was evidence of whether the faith was real.

So do not let either tribe define this for you. Biblical justice is neither a partisan slogan nor a threat to the gospel. It is the shape love takes when it reaches the gate where the powerless are waiting.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians agree Scripture commands justice and care for the vulnerable, but differ on how that translates into policy, how much is the work of the church versus the state, and which contemporary movements rightly carry the biblical word. The command is shared, the application contested.

questions.question: What is faith? Is it just believing without evidence?
questions.shortAnswer: No. Biblical faith is trust based on reasons, not a leap in the dark. It is the same kind of trust you place in a surgeon or a bridge, directed toward a God who has shown his character in history.
questions.answer:
The modern world has redefined faith as belief without evidence, even belief against the evidence, and then mocked Christians for having it. But that is not what the word means in the Bible, and it is not what believers across the centuries thought they were doing.

The Greek word translated faith, pistis, is better rendered trust or trustworthiness. It is a relational word. You have faith in a surgeon before an operation, not because you have no evidence, but because you have enough, her training, her record, the testimony of others, to place your life in her hands where you cannot see. Faith is what you do with knowledge that is real but incomplete, which is to say, faith is what you do with almost everything that matters.

The Bible never commends belief in a vacuum. When John the Baptist doubted, Jesus sent back a list of evidence. When the disciples doubted the resurrection, Jesus showed them his hands. Thomas asked to touch the wounds and was not rebuked for it. The apostles grounded their preaching in things they claimed to have seen and heard. The biblical writers appeal to public events, not private feelings.

This is why the old definition of faith as a blind leap gets it backward. Faith is not the absence of thinking. It is trust that commits the whole person, mind included, once it has seen enough to act. There is always a gap between the evidence and the commitment, because that is true of every relationship and every important decision in life. You never have total proof that your spouse loves you, or that the chair will hold. At some point you sit down. Faith is sitting down on what you have good reason to believe will hold.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how much weight to give reasoned argument versus the inner witness of the Spirit in coming to faith. Some emphasize evidences and apologetics, others the work of God on the heart that no argument can produce. Most hold that both play a part.

questions.question: Does God choose who is saved, or do we choose him?
questions.shortAnswer: Both streams run all through the Bible, and Christians have divided over how they fit for centuries. The honest answer holds God's sovereignty and real human responsibility together, even where we cannot fully reconcile them.
questions.answer:
This is one of the oldest and most heated debates in the church, and anyone who tells you it is simple is selling something. The reason it endures is that the Bible itself says both things, forcefully, often on the same page.

On one side are the passages that root salvation entirely in God's prior choice. Before the foundation of the world he chose his people. No one comes to Jesus unless the Father draws him. We love because he first loved us. This stream runs from Augustine, who battled Pelagius over whether we can take the first step toward God on our own, through the Reformers, into the tradition that bears Calvin's name. Its instinct is to protect grace: if any part of salvation finally depends on you, then you have something to boast about, and grace is no longer grace.

On the other side are the passages that plead, command, and warn, that hold people genuinely responsible for refusing. Choose this day. Whoever will, let him come. How often I longed to gather you, and you were not willing. This stream, associated with Arminius and much of the Wesleyan tradition, fears that if God secretly decided everything, then the invitations are theater and human choice is a fiction.

Faithful, brilliant Christians have stood on each side, and the debate will not be settled by a paragraph. What Scripture refuses to do is drop either truth. It never lets God's sovereignty erase your responsibility, and it never lets your choice dethrone God's grace. Charles Spurgeon, asked how he reconciled the two, said he never tried to reconcile friends. The practical counsel is older than the controversy: trust that salvation is God's work from first to last, and also know that the door is open and the call to come is sincere, addressed to you.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: This is the classic dividing line between the Reformed and Arminian traditions, with many positions in between. Reformed theology stresses unconditional election and grace that effectively saves; Arminian theology stresses God's universal offer and human freedom to accept or resist. Both affirm salvation is by grace through faith.

questions.question: What does the Bible actually mean by sin?
questions.shortAnswer: Far more than breaking rules. Sin is the deep disorder of a life turned in on itself instead of toward God, missing the mark of what we were made for. The behaviors are only the symptoms.
questions.answer:
Say the word sin and most people picture a list, mostly involving appetite and pleasure, the things a scold disapproves of. That cartoon makes the doctrine easy to dismiss. The biblical idea is larger, sadder, and harder to escape.

The main New Testament word, hamartia, is an archery term. It means to miss the mark, to fall short of a target. The mark we miss is the life we were made for, love of God and neighbor with the whole self. Sin is not first the breaking of an arbitrary rule. It is the failure to be what we are for, the way a knife that will not cut has failed, whatever else it does well.

Underneath the acts, the Bible locates a condition. Augustine described the human heart as incurvatus in se, curved in on itself, bending every good thing back toward the self as the center. On this account the root sin is not sensuality but pride, the quiet determination to be god in the place of God, to run my life as my own. The Ten Commandments begin where the disorder begins, with worship, because every other sin is a symptom of putting something other than God in the first place. The theologians call that idolatry, and it is the engine under the hood.

This is grim news, and Christianity does not flinch from it. We are not basically fine people who occasionally slip. We are people with a deep fault running through the center, capable of real good and real horror, often in the same week. But the diagnosis is the setup for the cure. A faith that told you that you were fine would have nothing to offer when you discovered you were not. The gospel takes the disease seriously enough to do something about it, which is why its honesty about sin and its hope about grace are not in tension. They are the same realism, seen from both sides.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on the precise effects of the fall, especially how far human nature is corrupted and how much capacity for good remains. Traditions range from total depravity to a more optimistic account of the image of God in fallen people. All hold that sin is universal and serious.

questions.question: Who, or what, is the Holy Spirit?
questions.shortAnswer: Not an impersonal force or a feeling, but the third person of the Trinity, fully God, who lives inside believers, makes them new, and binds the church together.
questions.answer:
The Holy Spirit is the member of the Trinity most people find hazy, often imagined as a vague energy or a warm feeling in a worship service. The Bible describes something far more personal and far more central than that.

First, the Spirit is a person, not a force. He can be grieved, lied to, and resisted, which a force cannot. He teaches, decides, and intercedes. The early church confessed at the Council of Constantinople in 381 that the Spirit is the Lord, the giver of life, worshiped together with the Father and the Son, fully God and not a junior partner or a created power.

Second, the Spirit is how God gets close. In the Old Testament the Spirit came upon particular people for particular tasks. After Pentecost, the astonishing claim is that God now lives inside ordinary believers, all of them, making the body a temple. Jesus told his followers it was actually better for them that he go away, because then the Spirit would come, not alongside them but within them. The distant God of the lightning and the mountain now indwells the people he saved.

Third, the Spirit does specific work. He convinces people of the truth about themselves and about Christ. He gives new birth, the inner change no argument can manufacture. He produces character over time, the fruit Paul lists, love, joy, peace, patience, and the rest. And he distributes gifts for building up the church. So when Christians speak of the Spirit, they are not talking about an atmosphere or a mood. They are talking about God himself, present and at work, finishing in us what the Father planned and the Son accomplished.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ over the miraculous gifts of the Spirit. Cessationists hold that gifts like tongues and prophecy ceased with the apostolic age; continuationists and Pentecostal and charismatic traditions hold they continue today. The shared confession is the Spirit's deity and his work in salvation and sanctification.
questions.doctrineTitle: The Holy Spirit and His Gifts

questions.question: How old is the earth, and does it matter?
questions.shortAnswer: Faithful Christians hold several views, from a young earth to billions of years, depending on how they read Genesis 1. The age of the earth is a real question, but it is not the center of the faith, and the resurrection does not hang on it.
questions.answer:
Few topics generate more heat with less light. Some Christians treat the age of the earth as a test of whether you take the Bible seriously, and some skeptics treat it as proof the Bible is nonsense. Both are claiming more certainty than the question warrants.

The debate turns on how to read the opening chapters of Genesis, which means the first question is not scientific but literary. What kind of writing is this. Christians who love the Bible equally have read it in several ways. Young-earth creationists read the six days as six ordinary days a few thousand years ago. Old-earth creationists read the days as long ages, or as a literary framework, and accept the scientific dating of the cosmos at roughly 13.8 billion years and the earth at about 4.5 billion. Still others read Genesis 1 as exalted theological poetry never meant to function as a science textbook at all, making claims about who made the world and why, not about mechanism and timetable.

It is worth remembering that this is not a modern panic invented to dodge science. Augustine, sixteen hundred years ago, warned against reading Genesis so woodenly that Christians embarrass the faith by contradicting what can actually be known about the natural world, and he speculated that creation might have been instantaneous, not spread over literal days. The instinct to read the text carefully rather than flatly is ancient.

Here is the proportion to keep. The Bible's central claims, that God made everything from nothing, that it was good, that humanity bears his image and has fallen, and supremely that Christ has risen, are not in question among these views. The faith was not built on a date. So hold your conviction about the age of the earth with honesty and humility, argue it as a secondary matter, and do not let it become a wall between you and people the resurrection should unite.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: This question is itself a place of significant disagreement. Young-earth, old-earth, and framework or literary readings of Genesis all have thoughtful Christian defenders. Views also differ on biological evolution. These are held as secondary matters that do not divide the core gospel.

questions.question: Doesn't the Bible support slavery?
questions.shortAnswer: It regulates an ancient institution rather than founding it, and it plants the very seeds that grew into abolition. But the honest reckoning includes the way the church later twisted it to defend a far worse evil.
questions.answer:
This is one of the heaviest charges against the Bible, and it must not be brushed aside, because professing Christians once used these texts to chain human beings. Any honest answer has to hold both the text and that history.

First, the slavery in the Bible is mostly not the race-based, lifelong, kidnapping-fueled slavery of the Atlantic trade. Much of it was closer to indentured servitude, a way the poor survived debt in a world with no welfare and no bankruptcy, often time-limited and entered to pay what was owed. That does not make it good. It makes it a different and lesser horror than the one the word conjures for us, and reading our system back into theirs distorts both.

Second, the law given to Israel restrained the institution in ways radical for its time. It demanded rest for servants, it made the kidnapping and selling of a person a capital crime, exactly what the Atlantic trade was built on, and it commanded release in the seventh year. The trajectory is toward limit and release, not toward entrenchment.

Third, and most important, the New Testament plants a charge under the whole institution that would eventually blow it apart. Paul tells masters and slaves they have the same Master in heaven who shows no favoritism. In the letter to Philemon he sends a runaway slave back not as property but as a beloved brother, which quietly detonates the logic of ownership. And the bedrock claim that every human bears God's image, and that in Christ there is neither slave nor free, is the seed from which abolition grew. It was Christians reading their own Bible, Wilberforce and the formerly enslaved preachers and the Quakers, who led the fight to end it.

So the church's record here is genuinely two-sided, and we should own both halves. Some used these pages to justify monstrous cruelty, twisting Scripture to bless their greed. Others, reading the same pages, heard the image of God in the people their society called property, and would not rest until the chains came off. The Bible did not invent slavery. It is the book that, taken to its conclusion, could not finally live with it.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how directly the New Testament condemns versus merely regulates slavery, and on how to read its instructions to slaves and masters. Nearly all today affirm that the Bible's deepest logic, the image of God and oneness in Christ, condemns slaveholding outright.

questions.question: Is depression or anxiety a sign of weak faith?
questions.shortAnswer: No. Some of the most faithful people in Scripture were crushed by despair. Mental illness is suffering, not sin, and reaching for a doctor is no more faithless than setting a broken bone.
questions.answer:
Too many believers carry a second wound on top of the first: they are depressed or anxious, and they have been told, or they assume, that a real Christian would not be. So the suffering becomes shameful, and the shame drives it underground, where it always gets worse. This teaching is cruel, and it is not in the Bible.

Scripture is full of faithful people in the pit. Elijah, just after his greatest victory, sat under a tree and asked God to let him die. David soaked his bed with tears and asked how long, over and over. The author of Psalm 88, a believer, ends in the dark with no sunrise in the final line, and God left that prayer in the book. Even Jesus, in Gethsemane, was sorrowful to the point of death. Whatever despair is, it is not proof that faith has failed.

It helps to make a few distinctions the old advice flattened. There is ordinary sorrow, which is healthy and right. There is the spiritual heaviness the older writers called the dark night, which can be a season of growth. And there is clinical depression and anxiety, which often have physical and chemical roots, the body's machinery misfiring, no more a moral failing than diabetes is. Confusing these does real damage, telling someone to pray harder when what they also need is treatment.

So treat the body as part of God's good creation. Reaching for a counselor, a doctor, or medication is not a failure of trust any more than wearing glasses is a failure to believe you can see. Many faithful believers walk with these conditions their whole lives and serve God anyway, sometimes most deeply because of what the darkness taught them. Grace does not require you to pretend you are fine. It meets you exactly where you actually are, in the pit, and it does not despise the rope, the friend, or the physician it sends down.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how to weigh spiritual and medical causes, and on the place of medication and professional therapy alongside prayer and the church. A growing consensus across traditions treats mental illness as real suffering calling for both spiritual and medical care.

questions.question: Will I see my loved ones again?
questions.shortAnswer: For those who die in Christ, the Bible's answer is yes, and not as ghosts or memories but as real people, raised and embodied, in a reunion meant to last. It treats this not as wishful thinking but as solid hope.
questions.answer:
This is rarely an abstract question. It is usually asked at a graveside, or in the quiet afterward, by someone who would trade everything for one more conversation. The Bible does not answer it with a shrug or a maybe. It answers with a hope it calls sure.

Paul wrote to grieving Christians precisely so they would not grieve like those who have no hope. Notice he did not tell them to stop grieving, he is not heartless about loss, but he gave them a reason their grief was not the end of the sentence. The dead in Christ will rise, he said, and then we will be together, and so we will always be with the Lord. He told them to comfort one another with those words. Reunion was not a sentiment he allowed. It was a doctrine he commanded them to lean on.

The shape of that reunion matters. The Christian hope is not disembodied souls recognizing each other as wisps. It is resurrection, real people with real bodies like the risen Jesus, who was recognized by his friends, who ate with them, who was unmistakably himself. Whatever else the new creation holds, it is not less personal and less embodied than this life. It is more.

There is an honest hard edge, and love does not lie about it. This hope is tied to Christ, for those who are his. The Bible will not promise a universal reunion irrespective of how anyone met God, and that is exactly why it presses on the living. The reunion you long for is real, and it is one more reason the gospel is urgent now, while there is still time to point the people you love toward the One who raises the dead.

But to the believer weeping over a believer, the word is steady and specific. You have not lost them into nothing. You have sent them ahead. And the parting that feels so final is, in the deepest reality, temporary. The God who defeated death has promised the table will be full again.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on the details of the intermediate state and on how much of earthly relationship carries into the resurrection. The shared, central hope is bodily resurrection and unbroken life together with God and his people.
